pages.title: Desk letter
pages.content:
Once a month the desk sends one short letter: a change in a tariff rule, a reminder of a cut-off, one thing we saw at the examination table. No advertising, no tracking.

To receive it, write to desk@shirushi-customs.example with the word “letter” in the subject line. To stop, write the same address.

Read the notes

posts.title: What goes on a packing list we can check in ten minutes
posts.excerpt: The few lines that let the desk check a packing list against the cartons without a single phone call.
posts.content:
A packing list is the document the desk reads first, and a good one is short. It names each carton by number, says what is inside in plain words, and gives a weight that matches the scale at the dock. When those three things line up, we can check the list against the goods in about ten minutes.

The lines that cost time are the vague ones: “parts”, “assorted”, “samples as agreed”. Say what the part is made of, what it is used for and how many there are. If two cartons hold the same item, say so, and give each carton its own line.

Send the packing list together with the commercial invoice. We read them against each other before anything else, because a mismatch found at the desk is a short e-mail, and the same mismatch found at the dock is a delay.

posts.title: Classification before you order
posts.excerpt: Why we give small manufacturers a tariff code and a short written reason before the first purchase order.
posts.content:
The tariff code decides the duty rate, whether a licence is needed and which declaration fits. Most workshops only learn it after the goods are on a ship. We prefer to settle it first, in writing, for each product.

A classification opinion from the desk is one page: the product as you describe it, the code we propose, the reason in two or three sentences and any doubt we still have. If the doubt matters, we say that the authority could be asked, and what that would involve.

Send a specification sheet and a photograph, not just a name. A turned wooden part and a finished table leg can share a name and still sit in different places in the tariff.

posts.title: Samples for a trade fair: temporary admission in plain words
posts.excerpt: Bringing samples in for a fair without paying duty on goods that will leave again.
posts.content:
Temporary admission lets goods enter for a fixed purpose, such as a trade fair, a test or a repair, and leave again without duty being paid. The goods must be identified, and they must go back.

We set up the admission before the cases are packed, list each sample with its description and value, and keep the record open until the goods have been re-exported. If something is sold at the fair, the entry is changed to a normal import for that item.

The most common problem is a sample that is not on the list. Check the cases against the list once more at the dock; that takes five minutes and saves a long conversation later.

posts.title: When goods are selected for examination
posts.excerpt: What happens at the steel table, who is there and what you will be told afterwards.
posts.content:
From time to time the authority selects a shipment for examination. It is routine, it is not an accusation, and it usually means a day or two rather than a week.

Our dock liaison goes to the table with the entry and the packing list. Cartons are opened, goods are checked against the declaration and put back. We tell you what was opened, what was found and whether anything has to change on the entry.

Pack so that a carton can be opened and closed again: no foam poured into the box, no taped-over lids that cannot be cut cleanly. Good packing is the best help we can give the examiner.

posts.title: Inward processing for small workshops
posts.excerpt: How a workshop that imports components and exports finished frames can avoid paying duty twice.
posts.content:
Inward processing is meant for goods that come in, are made into something else and leave again. A workshop that imports tubing and components and exports finished frames may be able to import them without duty.

The desk prepares the application, sets up the records the authority asks for and reconciles every entry against the authorisation. It is more paperwork than a normal entry, and it is worth it only when the volume is steady.

We usually start with a short call about what you import, what you make and where it goes, and then say plainly whether the route fits your business.

posts.title: Reading a duty notice
posts.excerpt: A duty notice has four numbers that matter. Here is where to find them and what each one means.
posts.content:
A duty notice looks dense, but four figures carry the meaning: the customs value, the duty rate, the import tax base and the total due. Everything else is a reference.

The customs value is not always the invoice value; freight and insurance are often added. The duty is a percentage of that value. The import tax is then calculated on value plus duty, which is why it is higher than people expect.

We show you the figures before they are paid and pass them through at cost, without mark-up. If a figure looks wrong to you, ask; a second reading costs nothing.
